case: A 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of fatigue, joint aches, and yellow discoloration of her eyes. She takes levothyroxine for Hashimoto thyroiditis and no other medications or supplements, and she does not drink alcohol. Temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8 °F), pulse is 82/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows scleral icterus and mild tender hepatomegaly. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 13.2 g/dL (normal 12.0 to 16.0), ALT 642 U/L (normal 7 to 56), AST 588 U/L (normal 10 to 40), alkaline phosphatase 148 U/L (normal 40 to 130), total bilirubin 4.1 mg/dL (normal 0.1 to 1.2), and serum IgG 2,650 mg/dL (normal 700 to 1,600). Serologic tests for hepatitis A, B, and C are negative. A liver biopsy is performed. Diagnosis: autoimmune hepatitis type 1.

questions.stem: Serum autoantibody testing is performed. Antibodies against which of the following antigens are most likely to be present?
options: Cytochrome P450 2D6
Gastric H+/K+ ATPase
Filamentous actin
Tissue transglutaminase
approach: Note the young woman with another autoimmune disease, high IgG, and a hepatitis pattern with negative viral serology: autoimmune hepatitis.
Recall that type 1 is marked by antinuclear and anti-smooth muscle antibodies, and type 2 by anti-LKM1.
Name the antigen that anti-smooth muscle antibodies recognize.
questions.why: Type 1 autoimmune hepatitis is defined by antinuclear antibodies and anti-smooth muscle antibodies. Anti-smooth muscle antibodies mainly recognize filamentous actin (F-actin), which is why they are also called anti-actin antibodies. The antibodies are markers of the disease; the liver damage itself is driven mainly by T cells. A high serum IgG is another typical finding.
whyNot: Anti-liver-kidney microsomal type 1 antibodies target cytochrome P450 2D6. They define autoimmune hepatitis type 2, which is seen mostly in children and adolescents.
Antibodies to the H+/K+ ATPase of parietal cells mark autoimmune gastritis, which causes atrophic body gastritis and pernicious anemia.
Correct.
Antibodies to tissue transglutaminase mark celiac disease, which injures the small bowel and causes malabsorption.

questions.stem: Her physician considers drug-induced liver injury, but she has taken no acetaminophen, isoniazid, or other hepatotoxic drugs. Which of the following findings on the liver biopsy is most likely and best distinguishes her disease from acetaminophen toxicity?
options: Interface hepatitis with portal plasma cell infiltrates
Centrilobular coagulative necrosis with little inflammation
Granulomatous destruction of interlobular bile ducts
Macrovesicular steatosis with Mallory-Denk bodies
approach: Recognize autoimmune hepatitis from the high IgG, other autoimmunity, and negative viral tests.
Recall its lesion: inflammation spilling from the portal tract into the lobule (interface hepatitis) rich in plasma cells.
Contrast this with acetaminophen injury, which is zone 3 necrosis with sparse inflammation.
questions.why: Autoimmune hepatitis shows interface hepatitis: lymphocytes and many plasma cells cross the limiting plate and destroy periportal hepatocytes. The plasma cells match the high serum IgG. Acetaminophen and other toxic injuries kill zone 3 hepatocytes around the central vein and cause little inflammation. Isoniazid hepatitis looks like viral hepatitis on biopsy, so history and serology matter as well.
whyNot: Correct.
Coagulative necrosis around the central vein (zone 3) with little inflammation is the pattern of acetaminophen toxicity. Zone 3 hepatocytes have the most cytochrome P450 2E1 and the least oxygen.
Granulomatous destruction of small interlobular bile ducts is the lesion of primary biliary cholangitis, which causes a cholestatic pattern with a high alkaline phosphatase.
Large fat droplets with Mallory-Denk bodies point to alcohol-related or metabolic liver disease. She does not drink, and her pattern is a high-transaminase hepatitis.

questions.stem: Urinalysis shows bilirubin and an increased concentration of urobilinogen. Which of the following best explains the increased urine urobilinogen in this patient?
options: Accelerated heme breakdown from red cell hemolysis
Complete obstruction of bile flow into the duodenum
Renal conversion of filtered conjugated bilirubin
Impaired hepatic reuptake of absorbed urobilinogen
approach: Recall that gut bacteria make urobilinogen, some of which is absorbed into portal blood and normally taken back up by the liver.
Hepatocyte injury reduces that reuptake, so more urobilinogen passes into the systemic blood and urine.
The bilirubin in her urine shows a conjugated component, which fits liver injury and argues against pure hemolysis.
questions.why: Bile still reaches the gut in hepatocellular injury, so bacteria keep making urobilinogen. Part of it is absorbed into portal blood, and a healthy liver takes most of it back up and re-excretes it in bile. Injured hepatocytes clear it poorly, so more spills into the urine. Conjugated bilirubin leaking from damaged cells is water soluble and also appears in the urine. Hemolysis raises urobilinogen without urine bilirubin, and complete obstruction makes urobilinogen disappear.
whyNot: Hemolysis raises urine urobilinogen by increasing bilirubin production, but urine bilirubin stays negative because the extra bilirubin is unconjugated. Her hemoglobin is normal and her urine contains bilirubin.
Complete obstruction stops bilirubin from reaching the gut, so no urobilinogen is formed and urine urobilinogen falls to zero.
Urobilinogen is made by gut bacteria from bilirubin in the intestinal lumen. The kidney does not convert bilirubin to urobilinogen.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her prothrombin time is 18 seconds (normal 11 to 13.5), and the platelet count is 240,000/mm3 (normal 150,000 to 400,000). The prothrombin time does not change after an intravenous dose of vitamin K. Which of the following best explains the prolonged prothrombin time?
options: Impaired micellar absorption of vitamin K from the gut
Reduced hepatocyte synthesis of clotting factors
Consumption of clotting factors in disseminated coagulation
Circulating autoantibody inhibitor directed at factor VIII
approach: The prothrombin time depends mostly on factor VII, plus factors X, V, II, and fibrinogen, all made by hepatocytes.
Separate a vitamin K problem from a synthesis problem by giving vitamin K by vein: only a vitamin K deficit corrects.
No correction with a normal platelet count means the liver cannot make the factors.
questions.why: Hepatocytes make almost all clotting factors. Factor VII has the shortest half-life, about 6 hours, so the prothrombin time rises within a day or so of severe liver injury. Giving vitamin K by vein corrects a prolonged prothrombin time caused by poor absorption, but not one caused by failing hepatocytes. A prothrombin time that does not correct marks severe hepatocyte dysfunction, along with a low albumin and a high ammonia.
whyNot: Poor absorption of vitamin K would be corrected by giving vitamin K intravenously, which bypasses the gut. Her prothrombin time did not change.
Correct.
Disseminated intravascular coagulation consumes factors and platelets together. Her platelet count is normal, and nothing suggests a trigger.
Factor VIII is in the intrinsic pathway, so an inhibitor prolongs the PTT, not the prothrombin time.

case: A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician because of an 8-month history of generalized itching that is worse at night, and fatigue. She also has dry eyes and a dry mouth. She does not drink alcohol and takes no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows excoriations on the arms and back, yellow plaques on both upper eyelids, and mild hepatomegaly. Laboratory studies show alkaline phosphatase 486 U/L (normal 40 to 130), GGT 390 U/L (normal 9 to 48), ALT 68 U/L (normal 7 to 56), total bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL (normal 0.1 to 1.2), and total cholesterol 310 mg/dL (desirable below 200). Ultrasonography shows normal extrahepatic bile ducts without dilation. Serologic tests for autoantibodies are sent. Diagnosis: primary biliary cholangitis.

questions.stem: A liver biopsy is performed. Which of the following findings is most likely?
options: Concentric onion-skin fibrosis around medium-sized bile ducts
Bile ductular proliferation with bile lakes and portal edema
Periportal hepatocytes with PAS-positive cytoplasmic globules
Granulomatous destruction of small interlobular bile ducts
approach: A middle-aged woman with pruritus, a high alkaline phosphatase, and normal extrahepatic ducts has intrahepatic cholestasis.
Primary biliary cholangitis targets the small interlobular ducts inside the portal tracts.
Its signature lesion is lymphocytic and granulomatous destruction of these ducts (the florid duct lesion).
questions.why: Primary biliary cholangitis is an autoimmune attack on small intrahepatic bile ducts. Lymphocytes and sometimes granulomas surround and destroy the interlobular ducts, and the ducts slowly disappear (ductopenia). Primary sclerosing cholangitis is different: it affects larger intrahepatic and extrahepatic ducts with onion-skin fibrosis, is linked to ulcerative colitis, and raises the risk of cholangiocarcinoma. Her dry eyes and mouth fit the Sjogren syndrome that often accompanies primary biliary cholangitis.
whyNot: Concentric onion-skin fibrosis around larger ducts is the lesion of primary sclerosing cholangitis, which usually affects men with ulcerative colitis and causes beaded ducts on cholangiography.
Ductular proliferation, portal edema, and bile lakes are the picture of large duct (extrahepatic) obstruction. Her ultrasound shows no duct dilation.
PAS-positive globules in periportal hepatocytes are misfolded alpha-1 antitrypsin, seen in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
Correct.

topics: Primary biliary versus primary sclerosing cholangitis

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her serum cholesterol concentration and eyelid plaques?
options: Loss of lipoprotein lipase activity in capillary beds
Retention of cholesterol normally excreted in bile
Increased intestinal absorption of dietary cholesterol
Defective LDL receptor-mediated uptake by hepatocytes
approach: Identify the cholestatic pattern: high alkaline phosphatase and GGT, pruritus, normal extrahepatic ducts.
Recall that bile is the body's main route for removing cholesterol, as free cholesterol and as bile acids.
When bile flow fails, biliary lipids back up into blood and are deposited in skin as xanthomas.
questions.why: The liver gets rid of cholesterol by secreting it into bile, both unchanged and after converting it to bile acids. In cholestasis this outflow is blocked, and biliary cholesterol and phospholipid reflux into the blood, partly as an abnormal particle called lipoprotein X. Serum cholesterol rises and is deposited in the skin as xanthelasma and xanthomas. A raised GGT along with the alkaline phosphatase confirms the alkaline phosphatase comes from the liver, not bone. Retained bile acids also contribute to the itching.
whyNot: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency raises chylomicrons and triglycerides and causes eruptive xanthomas and pancreatitis, not cholestatic hypercholesterolemia.
Correct.
Cholesterol absorption needs bile salt micelles. Cholestasis lowers intestinal bile salts, so absorption falls rather than rises.
LDL receptor defects (familial hypercholesterolemia) cause high LDL from birth with tendon xanthomas. Her cholesterol rose with a cholestatic liver disease.

questions.stem: Her disease progresses over several years with persistent cholestasis. Which of the following is she at greatest risk of developing as a result of reduced bile flow?
options: Impaired dark adaptation
Megaloblastic anemia
Perifollicular hemorrhages
Angular cheilitis and glossitis
approach: Bile salts form micelles that carry dietary fat and the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K to the enterocyte.
Chronic cholestasis therefore causes deficiency of these four vitamins, not of water-soluble vitamins.
Match the deficiency to its sign: vitamin A deficiency impairs rhodopsin regeneration, causing night blindness.
questions.why: Vitamins A, D, E, and K dissolve in fat and are absorbed inside bile salt micelles. Low bile flow in long-standing cholestasis causes fat malabsorption and deficiency of all four. Vitamin A is needed to make rhodopsin, so deficiency first shows as poor vision in dim light. The other deficiencies are osteomalacia (D), hemolytic anemia with neuropathy (E), and a prolonged prothrombin time (K). Water-soluble vitamins are absorbed without micelles.
whyNot: Correct.
Megaloblastic anemia comes from folate or vitamin B12 deficiency. These water-soluble vitamins do not need bile for absorption; B12 needs intrinsic factor and the terminal ileum.
Perifollicular hemorrhages are a sign of scurvy (vitamin C deficiency). Vitamin C is water soluble and absorbed without bile.
Angular cheilitis and glossitis point to riboflavin or other B vitamin deficiency, which does not depend on bile salts.

questions.stem: The autoantibody that is most characteristic of her disease is detected. Which of the following is the target antigen of this antibody?
options: Intrinsic factor secreted by gastric parietal cells
Double-stranded DNA in cell nuclei
E2 subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex
Thyroid peroxidase in follicular cells
approach: The characteristic antibody in primary biliary cholangitis is antimitochondrial antibody, present in about 95% of patients.
Recall its target: the E2 component of pyruvate dehydrogenase, an enzyme of the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Rule out antibodies that belong to other autoimmune diseases.
questions.why: Antimitochondrial antibodies are the serologic hallmark of primary biliary cholangitis. Their main target is the E2 subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC-E2). Bile duct epithelial cells display this antigen in a form that attracts an immune attack, which is thought to explain why the damage centers on small bile ducts. A positive antimitochondrial antibody with a cholestatic pattern is usually enough for the diagnosis without biopsy.
whyNot: Antibodies to intrinsic factor are found in autoimmune gastritis and cause vitamin B12 malabsorption and pernicious anemia.
Anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies are specific for systemic lupus erythematosus and track with lupus nephritis.
Correct.
Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies mark Hashimoto thyroiditis. They can occur with other autoimmune diseases but are not characteristic of this one.

case: A 19-year-old man comes to the physician because his roommate noticed that his eyes looked yellow. Over the past 3 days he had a febrile respiratory illness and ate very little. He has no abdominal pain, and his urine is normal in color. He takes no medications and does not drink alcohol. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 76/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows mild scleral icterus and no hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies show total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL (normal 0.1 to 1.2), direct bilirubin 0.2 mg/dL (normal 0 to 0.3), hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL (normal 13.5 to 17.5), and a reticulocyte count of 1% (normal 0.5 to 2.5). Haptoglobin, LDH, ALT, AST, and alkaline phosphatase are within normal limits. Diagnosis: Gilbert syndrome unmasked by fasting.

questions.stem: His newborn nephew develops severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that persists despite phototherapy and progresses to kernicterus. The nephew is found to have Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I. Which of the following best explains the difference in severity between the two conditions?
options: Normal versus defective canalicular MRP2 transport
Partial versus absent hepatic UGT1A1 activity
Normal versus accelerated red cell destruction
Normal versus deficient biliverdin reductase activity
approach: Both patients have isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia without hemolysis, so the problem is conjugation.
UGT1A1 attaches glucuronic acid to bilirubin. Gilbert syndrome has mildly reduced activity; Crigler-Najjar type I has none.
Relate the amount of residual enzyme to how high bilirubin rises and whether it reaches the brain.
questions.why: Gilbert syndrome is common and benign. Reduced expression of UGT1A1, often from a promoter variant, leaves roughly a third of normal activity, so bilirubin rises only mildly and mainly during fasting, stress, or illness. Crigler-Najjar type I has no UGT1A1 activity, so unconjugated bilirubin climbs high in the newborn period, crosses the immature blood-brain barrier, and causes kernicterus. Crigler-Najjar type II has partial deficiency and a milder course.
whyNot: MRP2 moves conjugated bilirubin into bile. Its defect causes Dubin-Johnson syndrome, a conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, which neither patient has.
Correct.
Neither condition involves hemolysis. Both are defects in bilirubin conjugation; this patient's hemoglobin, reticulocyte count, haptoglobin, and LDH are normal.
Biliverdin reductase converts biliverdin to bilirubin. A deficiency would lower bilirubin production, not cause unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

questions.stem: His urine remains normal in color despite the hyperbilirubinemia. Which of the following describes the form of his excess bilirubin in plasma that best explains this finding?
options: Conjugated to glucuronate and loosely bound to albumin
Free in plasma and reabsorbed by proximal tubules
Bound to haptoglobin and cleared by macrophages
Bound to albumin and not filtered
approach: His bilirubin is almost all indirect (unconjugated), since the direct fraction is normal.
Unconjugated bilirubin is water insoluble and travels in plasma tightly bound to albumin.
The albumin-bilirubin complex is too large to pass the glomerular filter, so no bilirubin enters the urine.
questions.why: Macrophages break heme into biliverdin with heme oxygenase, and biliverdin reductase converts it to unconjugated bilirubin. Unconjugated bilirubin is not water soluble, so it is carried to the liver bound to albumin and cannot be filtered by the kidney. That is why jaundice from unconjugated bilirubin is called acholuric. After hepatocytes conjugate it with UGT1A1, MRP2 pumps it into bile, and gut bacteria turn it into urobilinogen and stercobilin.
whyNot: Conjugated bilirubin is water soluble and only loosely bound to albumin, so when it is high it is filtered and appears in urine. His excess bilirubin is unconjugated.
Unconjugated bilirubin in plasma is almost entirely bound to albumin. It is not filtered and then reabsorbed.
Haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin, not bilirubin. Hemoglobin-haptoglobin complexes are cleared by macrophages.
Correct.

questions.stem: Once his bilirubin is conjugated, hepatocytes secrete it into bile canaliculi. Within the hepatic lobule, which of the following best describes the flow of this bile?
options: Toward the central vein, in the same direction as sinusoidal blood flow
Into the space of Disse, then into hepatic lymphatic vessels
Toward the portal triad, opposite to sinusoidal blood flow
Into the sinusoid lumen, then to the central vein
approach: Picture the classic lobule: portal triads at the corners and a central vein in the middle.
Blood from the portal vein and hepatic artery flows through sinusoids from the triad to the central vein.
Canaliculi between hepatocytes carry bile in the opposite direction, through the canals of Hering to the bile ductules of the portal triad.
questions.why: In the hepatic lobule, blood enters at the portal triad and flows through sinusoids to the central vein. Bile canaliculi, formed by grooves between adjacent hepatocytes and sealed by tight junctions, carry bile the other way. They drain through the canals of Hering into the bile ductules of the portal triad. The two flows run in opposite directions and never mix in health.
whyNot: Blood moves from the portal triad toward the central vein. Bile moves the other way, so it does not travel with the blood toward the central vein.
The space of Disse lies between hepatocytes and sinusoidal endothelium and drains to lymphatics, but it carries plasma filtrate, not bile.
Correct.
Bile is kept apart from blood by tight junctions around the canaliculi, and it drains toward the portal triad rather than into the sinusoids.

topics: Bile canaliculi and canals of Hering

questions.stem: During his 3 days of poor intake, his serum beta-hydroxybutyrate concentration rose. Which of the following best explains why his liver, which produced these ketone bodies, did not oxidize them for its own energy?
options: Hepatocytes lack succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase
Hepatocytes lack mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase activity
Hepatic mitochondria lack carnitine palmitoyltransferase I
Ketone bodies cannot cross the hepatocyte plasma membrane
approach: In fasting, the liver oxidizes fatty acids to acetyl-CoA and turns the excess into acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate.
To use acetoacetate, a tissue must first convert it to acetoacetyl-CoA with succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase (thiophorase).
The liver lacks this enzyme, so it exports ketones to other tissues.
questions.why: In fasting, liver glycogen runs low within about a day, and blood glucose then depends on gluconeogenesis from alanine, lactate, and glycerol. At the same time, the liver oxidizes fatty acids and converts the extra acetyl-CoA into ketone bodies. Muscle, heart, and brain use ketones after converting acetoacetate to acetoacetyl-CoA with thiophorase. The liver lacks thiophorase, so it can make ketones but not use them, and they are exported as fuel.
whyNot: Correct.
Hepatocytes have mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase. It is the rate-limiting enzyme of ketone body synthesis, which is why the liver can make ketones.
Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I brings fatty acids into hepatic mitochondria. The liver needs it to make ketones in the first place.
Ketone bodies move freely across cell membranes. That is how they leave the liver for muscle and brain.

case: A 26-year-old woman comes to the physician because of yellow eyes for 4 weeks. She has had brief episodes of mild jaundice since adolescence. Three months ago she started an oral contraceptive. She has no pruritus or abdominal pain and does not drink alcohol. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows mild scleral icterus; the liver and spleen are not enlarged. Laboratory studies show total bilirubin 3.8 mg/dL (normal 0.1 to 1.2), direct bilirubin 2.6 mg/dL (normal 0 to 0.3), and a hemoglobin concentration of 13.6 g/dL (normal 12.0 to 16.0). ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, and GGT are within normal limits. Ultrasonography shows a normal gallbladder and no bile duct dilation. A liver biopsy is performed. Diagnosis: Dubin-Johnson syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following biopsy findings is most likely and distinguishes her condition from Rotor syndrome?
options: Coarse dark pigment within hepatocyte lysosomes
Hemosiderin granules in periportal hepatocytes and bile ducts
Copper-associated protein granules in periportal hepatocytes
Normal hepatocyte morphology with no pigment accumulation
approach: Isolated conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal liver enzymes and ducts suggests an inherited excretion defect.
Dubin-Johnson syndrome (MRP2 defect) and Rotor syndrome look alike in the blood.
Only Dubin-Johnson syndrome leaves dark pigment in the liver.
questions.why: Dubin-Johnson syndrome is an autosomal recessive defect in MRP2, the canalicular pump that moves conjugated bilirubin and other organic anions into bile. Conjugated bilirubin backs up into the blood. A dark, melanin-like pigment collects in hepatocyte lysosomes and makes the liver look black. Rotor syndrome causes a similar but milder conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with a normal, unpigmented liver. Estrogens and pregnancy reduce biliary excretion further, which is why her jaundice worsened on an oral contraceptive.
whyNot: Correct.
Hemosiderin in periportal hepatocytes is the pattern of hereditary hemochromatosis, which raises transaminases and ferritin rather than causing isolated conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
Periportal copper and copper-associated protein are seen in Wilson disease and in long-standing cholestasis. Neither fits her isolated conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal enzymes.
A normal, unpigmented liver is the finding in Rotor syndrome, the milder look-alike of Dubin-Johnson syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following urinalysis results is most likely in this patient?
options: Bilirubin absent; urobilinogen increased
Bilirubin present; urobilinogen absent
Bilirubin present; urobilinogen normal
Bilirubin absent; urobilinogen normal
approach: Her raised bilirubin is mostly direct (conjugated), and conjugated bilirubin is water soluble and filtered at the glomerulus, so urine bilirubin is present.
Urobilinogen depends on bilirubin reaching the gut. Her ducts are open, so bacteria still make urobilinogen.
With normal liver cells to reclaim it, urine urobilinogen stays about normal.
questions.why: Conjugated bilirubin is water soluble and only loosely bound to albumin, so it passes into the urine when its blood level rises. In Dubin-Johnson syndrome bile still reaches the intestine, and hepatocytes are otherwise healthy, so urobilinogen formation and reuptake are about normal. This combination separates it from hemolysis (no urine bilirubin, high urobilinogen) and complete obstruction (urine bilirubin with absent urobilinogen).
whyNot: No urine bilirubin with high urobilinogen is the pattern of hemolysis, in which the extra bilirubin is unconjugated. Her hemoglobin is normal and her bilirubin is mostly direct.
Bilirubin with no urobilinogen means bile is not reaching the gut, as in complete obstruction. Her ducts are normal and bile still flows.
Correct.
Absent urine bilirubin fits normal people and unconjugated causes such as Gilbert syndrome. Her bilirubin is mostly conjugated.

questions.stem: Her normal ultrasound argued against biliary obstruction. Progressive obstruction by a tumor at which of the following sites would cause jaundice together with a distended gallbladder?
options: Common hepatic duct proximal to the cystic duct junction
Distal common bile duct within the pancreatic head
Cystic duct at the neck of the gallbladder
Right hepatic duct at the porta hepatis
approach: Trace bile: right and left hepatic ducts to the common hepatic duct, which joins the cystic duct to form the common bile duct.
The common bile duct runs through the head of the pancreas to the ampulla of Vater, where it joins the pancreatic duct under the sphincter of Oddi.
Only a block below the cystic duct junction both stops all bile flow and lets bile back up into the gallbladder.
questions.why: Bile leaves the liver through the right and left hepatic ducts at the porta hepatis, which join as the common hepatic duct. The cystic duct from the gallbladder joins it to form the common bile duct. This duct passes behind the duodenum and through the pancreatic head to the ampulla of Vater. Slow obstruction of the distal common bile duct, as by pancreatic head cancer, blocks all bile flow and lets the gallbladder fill and distend. This is the basis of Courvoisier sign.
whyNot: Obstruction of the common hepatic duct above the cystic duct causes jaundice, but bile cannot back up into the gallbladder, so it stays small.
Correct.
Cystic duct obstruction distends the gallbladder, but bile from the liver still flows down the common bile duct, so there is no jaundice.
Blocking one hepatic duct leaves the other lobe draining normally, so jaundice usually does not occur, and the gallbladder is not distended.

questions.stem: Which of the following sets of laboratory findings is most likely in this patient?
options: Low albumin, prolonged PT, high ammonia
Normal albumin, prolonged PT, high ammonia
Low albumin, normal PT, normal ammonia
Normal albumin, normal PT, normal ammonia
approach: Dubin-Johnson syndrome affects one transport step: moving conjugated bilirubin into bile.
Synthetic and metabolic work of the liver (albumin, clotting factors, urea cycle) is untouched.
So albumin, prothrombin time, and ammonia stay normal, unlike in liver failure.
questions.why: The liver makes albumin and most clotting factors and removes ammonia by turning it into urea. When hepatocytes fail, albumin falls, the prothrombin time lengthens, and ammonia rises, leading to edema, bleeding, and encephalopathy. Dubin-Johnson syndrome is a single transporter defect, so these functions are normal. This is why it is a benign condition that needs no treatment.
whyNot: Low albumin, a prolonged PT, and high ammonia together signal failing hepatocytes, as in cirrhosis or acute liver failure. Her hepatocytes are otherwise healthy.
A prolonged PT with high ammonia but normal albumin can occur early in acute liver failure because albumin has a long half-life. Her normal transaminases rule out such injury.
Low albumin with normal liver function suggests protein loss in the urine or gut, or malnutrition, not an inherited excretion defect.
Correct.

dx: Alcohol-related cirrhosis with spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and hepatorenal syndrome
case: A 58-year-old man with a 30-year history of heavy alcohol use is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-week history of increasing abdominal girth, fever, mild diffuse abdominal pain, and decreased urine output. Temperature is 38.2 °C (100.8 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg. Physical examination shows jaundice, spider angiomas, gynecomastia, and tense ascites with mild diffuse tenderness; there is no rigidity or guarding. Serum albumin is 2.4 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.5), and creatinine is 2.6 mg/dL (normal 0.7 to 1.3; 0.9 three months ago). Urine sodium is below 10 mEq/L, and urinalysis shows no protein, blood, or casts. Paracentesis shows ascitic albumin 0.8 g/dL and 620 neutrophils/mm3. Diagnosis: alcohol-related cirrhosis with spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and hepatorenal syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the serum-ascites albumin gradient in this patient?
options: Exudation of protein from inflamed peritoneum
Peritoneal seeding by metastatic carcinoma
High sinusoidal pressure from portal hypertension
Low oncotic pressure from glomerular albumin loss
approach: Calculate the gradient: serum albumin 2.4 minus ascitic albumin 0.8 equals 1.6 g/dL.
A gradient of 1.1 g/dL or more means the fluid formed from high hydrostatic pressure in the portal circulation.
In cirrhosis, fibrosis raises sinusoidal pressure; low albumin and sodium retention add to fluid build-up.
questions.why: The serum-ascites albumin gradient reflects the hydrostatic pressure pushing fluid out of the sinusoids. A value of 1.1 g/dL or more indicates portal hypertension, as in cirrhosis, Budd-Chiari syndrome, or heart failure. Ascites in cirrhosis forms from high sinusoidal pressure plus low oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminemia. Splanchnic vasodilation lowers effective arterial volume, which activates renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and makes the kidney retain sodium and water.
whyNot: Peritoneal inflammation, as in tuberculous peritonitis, adds protein to the fluid and gives a gradient below 1.1 g/dL. Infection of portal hypertensive ascites does not change the gradient much.
Peritoneal carcinomatosis makes a protein-rich exudate with a gradient below 1.1 g/dL.
Correct.
Nephrotic syndrome causes ascites through low oncotic pressure, but the gradient is below 1.1 g/dL. His urinalysis shows no protein.

questions.stem: Culture of the ascitic fluid grows Escherichia coli only. Which of the following best explains how this organism most likely reached the ascitic fluid?
options: Leakage of colonic flora through a perforated diverticulum
Direct inoculation during an earlier paracentesis
Rupture of a pyogenic abscess through the liver capsule
Translocation of gut bacteria into lymph and blood
approach: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is infection of ascites with no surgical source, diagnosed by 250 or more neutrophils/mm3.
It is usually one enteric gram-negative organism, most often E. coli or Klebsiella.
In cirrhosis, gut bacteria cross a leaky bowel wall into mesenteric lymph and blood and seed ascites that has poor opsonic activity.
questions.why: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis develops in cirrhotic ascites without a perforation or abscess. Bacterial overgrowth, a leaky gut wall, and impaired immune defenses let gut bacteria move into mesenteric lymph nodes and the blood. Ascites with a low protein level has little complement and opsonic activity, so the bacteria grow. Secondary peritonitis comes from a perforated or inflamed viscus, is polymicrobial, and causes a rigid abdomen. SBP is a common trigger of hepatorenal syndrome.
whyNot: A perforated viscus causes secondary peritonitis: polymicrobial flora including anaerobes, and a rigid abdomen with guarding. He has a single organism and no rigidity.
Infection from a needle puncture is rare and would more likely involve skin flora such as staphylococci, not a single enteric gram-negative rod.
A ruptured liver abscess is a cause of secondary peritonitis and would usually show an abscess on imaging and often mixed organisms.
Correct.

questions.stem: His creatinine does not improve after 2 days of intravenous albumin, and kidney ultrasonography is normal. Which of the following best explains his decline in renal function?
options: Renal vasoconstriction driven by splanchnic vasodilation
Ischemic acute tubular necrosis with shed epithelial casts
Immune complex glomerulonephritis from bacterial antigens
Allergic interstitial nephritis with eosinophiluria
approach: Kidney failure in advanced cirrhosis with low urine sodium, bland urine, and no response to volume expansion is hepatorenal syndrome.
Portal hypertension causes splanchnic arterial vasodilation (nitric oxide), which lowers effective arterial blood volume.
The body responds with renin-angiotensin, sympathetic, and vasopressin activation that intensely constricts renal arteries.
questions.why: Hepatorenal syndrome is a functional kidney failure. Splanchnic vessels dilate in portal hypertension, so the effective arterial volume falls even though total body fluid is high. Strong renin-angiotensin, sympathetic, and vasopressin activity then constricts the renal arteries and lowers the glomerular filtration rate. The kidneys are normal on histology and recover after liver transplant. Low urine sodium shows the tubules still work.
whyNot: Correct.
Acute tubular necrosis damages tubules, so urine sodium is high and the urine contains muddy brown casts. His urine sodium is below 10 mEq/L and the sediment is bland.
Glomerulonephritis would show hematuria, red cell casts, or protein in the urine. His urinalysis is clean.
Interstitial nephritis is usually a reaction to a drug and shows white cells and white cell casts in the urine. Nothing suggests a drug exposure, and his urinalysis is bland.

questions.stem: Physical examination also shows dilated veins radiating from the umbilicus. The collateral veins that carry portal blood to these surface veins reach the anterior abdominal wall within which of the following peritoneal folds?
options: Gastrohepatic ligament
Falciform ligament
Gastrosplenic ligament
Splenorenal ligament
approach: Dilated periumbilical veins (caput medusae) form when portal blood flows out through paraumbilical veins.
The paraumbilical veins run with the ligamentum teres, the remnant of the umbilical vein.
The ligamentum teres lies in the free lower edge of the falciform ligament, which runs from the liver to the umbilicus.
questions.why: The falciform ligament attaches the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and carries the ligamentum teres and the small paraumbilical veins in its free edge. In portal hypertension these veins open up and carry portal blood to the superficial veins around the umbilicus, producing caput medusae. Each of the other ligaments carries a different set of vessels: gastric arteries in the gastrohepatic, short gastrics in the gastrosplenic, and the splenic vessels with the pancreatic tail in the splenorenal.
whyNot: The gastrohepatic ligament, part of the lesser omentum, carries the left and right gastric vessels along the lesser curvature.
Correct.
The gastrosplenic ligament carries the short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels.
The splenorenal ligament carries the splenic artery and vein and the tail of the pancreas.

dx: Hypervitaminosis A with noncirrhotic portal hypertension
case: A 44-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of increasing abdominal girth, dry skin, hair loss, and bone pain. For 2 years he has taken about 100,000 IU of vitamin A daily to improve his skin. He does not drink alcohol. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows dry, scaly skin, splenomegaly, and shifting dullness. Platelet count is 92,000/mm3 (normal 150,000 to 400,000). ALT is 74 U/L (normal 7 to 56), and albumin is 3.8 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.5). Doppler ultrasonography shows ascites, splenomegaly, and patent portal and hepatic veins. A liver biopsy shows perisinusoidal fibrosis and hypertrophied fat-storing cells containing lipid droplets, without nodular cirrhosis. Diagnosis: hypervitaminosis A with noncirrhotic portal hypertension.

questions.stem: He also reports daily headaches and episodes of blurred vision. Which of the following findings is most likely on further evaluation?
options: Raised serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration
Raised cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure
Low serum ceruloplasmin concentration
Low serum vitamin B12 concentration
approach: Link the chronic high vitamin A intake to his skin, bone, and liver findings.
Recall that vitamin A toxicity raises intracranial pressure (pseudotumor cerebri), causing headache, papilledema, and blurred vision.
Raised intracranial pressure shows up as a high cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure on lumbar puncture.
questions.why: Chronic vitamin A excess causes dry skin, hair loss, bone pain, liver injury, and raised intracranial pressure. The headache and transient blurring of vision come from idiopathic intracranial hypertension, with papilledema and a high opening pressure. Vitamin A is also strongly teratogenic. Vitamin D toxicity looks different: hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, kidney stones, and polyuria.
whyNot: Raised 25-hydroxyvitamin D would point to vitamin D excess, which causes hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, and kidney stones. He took vitamin A only.
Correct.
Low ceruloplasmin suggests Wilson disease, which causes liver and neuropsychiatric disease, but not this vitamin A picture or raised intracranial pressure.
Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neuropathy, not headache with visual blurring from raised intracranial pressure.

topics: Vitamin A versus vitamin D toxicity

questions.stem: Which of the following cells is responsible for the fibrosis in this patient's liver, and where is it located?
options: Stellate cells in the space of Disse
Kupffer cells within the sinusoid lumen
Cholangiocytes lining the canals of Hering
Endothelial cells lining hepatic sinusoids
approach: The biopsy describes fat-storing cells next to the sinusoids. These are hepatic stellate (Ito) cells.
Stellate cells sit in the space of Disse and normally store vitamin A in lipid droplets.
When activated, they become myofibroblasts and deposit collagen, causing perisinusoidal fibrosis.
questions.why: Hepatic stellate (Ito) cells live in the space of Disse, between hepatocytes and the sinusoidal endothelium. At rest they store vitamin A in lipid droplets. Excess vitamin A loads and activates them, and activated stellate cells turn into myofibroblasts that lay down collagen in the space of Disse. This perisinusoidal fibrosis raises resistance to sinusoidal flow and can cause portal hypertension before cirrhosis develops. The same cell drives fibrosis in alcohol-related and viral liver disease.
whyNot: Correct.
Kupffer cells are resident macrophages in the sinusoids. They release cytokines that activate stellate cells but do not lay down most of the collagen.
Cholangiocytes line the bile ductules and canals of Hering. They proliferate in biliary disease but are not the main collagen-producing cells.
Sinusoidal endothelial cells are fenestrated and lack a basement membrane. They lose their fenestrae in fibrosis but do not make the scar.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions causes portal hypertension at the same anatomic level as in this patient?
options: Portal vein thrombosis
Budd-Chiari syndrome
Constrictive pericarditis
Alcohol-related cirrhosis
approach: His portal and hepatic veins are patent, so the block is inside the liver.
The biopsy shows perisinusoidal fibrosis, an intrahepatic cause.
Choose the option that also raises resistance inside the liver: cirrhosis.
questions.why: Portal hypertension is classified by where the resistance lies. Prehepatic causes block the portal vein, as in thrombosis. Intrahepatic causes raise resistance within the liver, as in cirrhosis, schistosomiasis, and perisinusoidal fibrosis from vitamin A. Posthepatic causes block outflow, as in Budd-Chiari syndrome, right heart failure, and constrictive pericarditis. All levels can cause splenomegaly and varices; ascites is typical of sinusoidal and posthepatic causes.
whyNot: Portal vein thrombosis blocks flow before blood reaches the liver. This is prehepatic portal hypertension.
Budd-Chiari syndrome is thrombosis of the hepatic veins, which blocks outflow after the liver. This is posthepatic portal hypertension.
Constrictive pericarditis raises right atrial and hepatic vein pressure. This is posthepatic portal hypertension.
Correct.

questions.stem: His splenomegaly results from raised pressure transmitted back from the portal vein. Which of the following describes the normal course of the vein that carries this pressure to the spleen?
options: Joins the inferior vena cava behind the second part of the duodenum
Joins the left renal vein anterior to the abdominal aorta
Joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the pancreatic neck
Joins the inferior mesenteric vein at the duodenojejunal flexure
approach: The spleen drains through the splenic vein, which runs behind the pancreas.
The splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the neck of the pancreas to form the portal vein.
High portal pressure is therefore transmitted directly back to the spleen, causing congestive splenomegaly.
questions.why: The splenic vein runs along the back of the pancreas and joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the pancreatic neck to form the portal vein. The portal vein carries this blood to the liver sinusoids, which drain through central veins to the hepatic veins and the inferior vena cava. When resistance rises in the liver, pressure backs up through the splenic vein into the spleen. The enlarged spleen traps platelets, explaining his thrombocytopenia.
whyNot: The splenic vein drains to the portal system, not the inferior vena cava. Portal blood reaches the vena cava only after passing through the liver.
The left renal vein crosses anterior to the aorta, but the splenic vein does not join it. A splenorenal connection exists only as a surgical shunt or a spontaneous collateral.
Correct.
The inferior mesenteric vein usually drains into the splenic vein, not the reverse, and the junction is behind the pancreas.

dx: Esophageal variceal hemorrhage in hepatitis C cirrhosis
case: A 61-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after vomiting a large amount of bright red blood. He has no abdominal or chest pain. He has chronic hepatitis C infection, acquired through injection drug use 30 years ago and never treated, and cirrhosis diagnosed 2 years ago. Temperature is 36.6 °C (97.9 °F), pulse is 124/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 84/50 mm Hg. Physical examination shows jaundice, splenomegaly, and ascites. Hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL (normal 13.5 to 17.5), and platelet count is 68,000/mm3 (normal 150,000 to 400,000). Upper endoscopy shows large actively bleeding varices in the distal esophagus. Diagnosis: esophageal variceal hemorrhage in hepatitis C cirrhosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why these veins dilated?
options: Azygos blood diverted via esophageal veins into the portal vein
Pressure transmitted upward from an obstructed superior vena cava
Erosive esophagitis weakening the walls of submucosal veins
Portal blood diverted via the left gastric vein to the azygos
approach: Cirrhosis raises portal pressure, so portal blood seeks lower-pressure systemic routes.
The left gastric (coronary) vein connects with esophageal veins that drain to the azygos system.
Extra flow dilates the thin submucosal veins of the distal esophagus, which can rupture and bleed massively.
questions.why: In portal hypertension, blood from the portal system flows backward through the left gastric vein into the esophageal venous plexus, which drains to the azygos system. The thin-walled submucosal veins of the distal esophagus dilate into varices. When they rupture, bleeding is painless and often massive. Variceal hemorrhage is one of the leading causes of death in cirrhosis, and low platelets and clotting factors make it worse.
whyNot: Flow goes from high to low pressure. In portal hypertension, blood moves from the portal side toward the systemic azygos side, not the reverse.
Superior vena cava obstruction can cause downhill varices in the upper esophagus, but he has cirrhosis with portal hypertension and distal varices.
Esophagitis damages mucosa and can bleed, but it does not cause the vein dilation of varices.
Correct.

questions.stem: Proctoscopy shows anorectal varices. These varices connect a portal tributary with the middle and inferior rectal veins. Which of the following is the portal tributary involved?
options: Internal pudendal vein
Inferior vesical vein
Superior rectal vein
Median sacral vein
approach: Portosystemic anastomoses form where portal and systemic veins meet.
The middle and inferior rectal veins drain to the internal iliac system (systemic).
The portal partner in the rectum is the superior rectal vein, a tributary of the inferior mesenteric vein.
questions.why: The rectum has a portal and a systemic venous drainage. The superior rectal vein drains to the inferior mesenteric vein and then the portal system. The middle rectal vein drains to the internal iliac vein, and the inferior rectal vein drains through the internal pudendal vein to the internal iliac vein. In portal hypertension, blood flows from the superior rectal vein into these systemic veins, forming anorectal varices. The other main sites are the esophagus (left gastric to azygos) and the umbilicus (paraumbilical to abdominal wall veins).
whyNot: The internal pudendal vein receives the inferior rectal vein and drains to the internal iliac vein. It is on the systemic side.
The inferior vesical vein drains the bladder to the internal iliac vein. It is systemic and not part of this anastomosis.
Correct.
The median sacral vein drains to the common iliac vein. It is systemic and not part of this anastomosis.

questions.stem: A year earlier he had palpable purpura on both legs, arthralgias, and hematuria with proteinuria. Serum C4 was low. Which of the following best explains these findings?
options: Galactose-deficient IgA1 complexes in small vessel walls
Cold-precipitating IgM rheumatoid factor-IgG complexes
Autoantibodies to neutrophil cytoplasmic myeloperoxidase
Antibodies to type IV collagen in basement membranes
approach: Chronic hepatitis C stimulates B cells, which can make monoclonal IgM with rheumatoid factor activity.
This IgM binds IgG (often with HCV antigen) to form complexes that precipitate in the cold: mixed cryoglobulins.
The complexes deposit in small vessels and glomeruli and fix complement, causing purpura, arthralgia, glomerulonephritis, and low C4.
questions.why: Most adults infected with HCV, about 75 to 85%, develop chronic infection, and a minority progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma over decades. Chronic infection also drives B cells to make IgM rheumatoid factor that binds IgG and viral antigen. These mixed cryoglobulins precipitate in cooler tissues and deposit in small vessels and glomeruli, consuming complement. The result is palpable purpura, arthralgias, and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.
whyNot: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) causes palpable purpura and nephritis, but usually in children, with normal complement and no rheumatoid factor.
Correct.
Myeloperoxidase ANCA vasculitis (microscopic polyangiitis) is pauci-immune, so complement is not consumed.
Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease affects the kidney and lung and does not cause purpura with low complement and rheumatoid factor.

questions.stem: No vaccine is available to prevent infection with this virus. Which of the following features of the virus best explains this?
options: Rapid variation of envelope glycoprotein epitopes
Integration of viral DNA into the host genome
Dependence on a helper virus for envelope proteins
Lack of a lipid envelope on the virion
approach: HCV is an enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA flavivirus.
Its RNA-dependent RNA polymerase has no proofreading, so mutations build up fast.
The envelope glycoproteins change constantly, so antibodies made against one variant miss the next, and vaccine design has failed.
questions.why: Hepatitis C virus is a flavivirus with an RNA genome. Its RNA-dependent RNA polymerase makes many errors and cannot proofread, so each patient carries a swarm of related variants (quasispecies). The hypervariable regions of the envelope glycoproteins keep changing and escape neutralizing antibodies. This explains both the high rate of chronic infection and the lack of a vaccine. Hepatitis B, by contrast, is a partially double-stranded DNA hepadnavirus with a stable surface antigen used in its vaccine.
whyNot: Correct.
Integration of viral DNA describes hepatitis B, which nonetheless has an effective vaccine. HCV is an RNA virus with no DNA stage.
Dependence on a helper virus describes hepatitis D, which needs HBsAg from hepatitis B. Vaccinating against hepatitis B prevents it.
Lack of an envelope describes hepatitis A and E, which spread by the fecal-oral route. Hepatitis A has an effective vaccine.

dx: Acute hepatitis B in an adult
case: A 34-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 10-day history of fatigue, nausea, right upper quadrant discomfort, and dark urine. Three months ago he had unprotected sexual intercourse with a new partner. Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 122/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows jaundice and tender hepatomegaly. Laboratory studies show ALT 1,840 U/L (normal 7 to 56), AST 1,210 U/L (normal 10 to 40), alkaline phosphatase 160 U/L (normal 40 to 130), total bilirubin 6.2 mg/dL (normal 0.1 to 1.2), direct bilirubin 4.5 mg/dL (normal 0 to 0.3), and prothrombin time 13 seconds (normal 11 to 13.5). HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc are positive; anti-HBs is negative. Tests for hepatitis A IgM and hepatitis C antibody are negative. Diagnosis: acute hepatitis B.

questions.stem: Eight weeks later his symptoms have resolved. Serologic testing now shows HBsAg negative, anti-HBs negative, and IgM anti-HBc positive. Which of the following best describes his status?
options: Window period of acute infection
Resolved infection with immunity
Chronic infection with low replication
Early acute infection before antibodies appear
approach: HBsAg has cleared, but anti-HBs has not yet appeared.
In this gap, IgM anti-HBc is the only positive marker.
This is the window period, which still means recent acute infection.
questions.why: In acute hepatitis B, HBsAg appears first and IgM anti-HBc follows with symptoms. As the infection clears, HBsAg disappears, and there can be a gap of weeks before anti-HBs becomes detectable. During this window period, IgM anti-HBc is the only marker, so it must be tested to avoid missing the infection. Recovery is later marked by anti-HBs and IgG anti-HBc. HBsAg lasting more than 6 months defines chronic infection.
whyNot: Correct.
Resolved infection shows anti-HBs with IgG anti-HBc. He has no anti-HBs yet, and his anti-HBc is still IgM.
Chronic infection requires HBsAg persisting longer than 6 months, with IgG anti-HBc. His HBsAg has already cleared.
Early acute infection shows HBsAg before any antibody. His HBsAg is gone and IgM anti-HBc is present.

questions.stem: Which of the following is mainly responsible for the hepatocyte injury in this patient?
options: Direct cytopathic lysis of hepatocytes by replicating virus
Complement-mediated lysis by antibody bound to infected cells
Toxic accumulation of HBsAg in hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum
CD8 T cells recognizing viral peptides on MHC class I
approach: HBV itself does little direct damage to the cells it infects.
Infected hepatocytes present viral peptides on MHC class I.
Cytotoxic CD8 T cells recognize these peptides and kill the cells, which raises ALT and also clears the virus.
questions.why: The liver damage in hepatitis B comes mainly from the immune response. Cytotoxic CD8 T cells recognize HBV peptides on MHC class I and kill infected hepatocytes by perforin, granzymes, and Fas ligand. Adults with a strong T cell response have marked ALT elevation but usually clear the virus. Newborns mount a weak response, have little injury, and most become chronically infected. Circulating HBsAg immune complexes can also cause polyarteritis nodosa and membranous nephropathy.
whyNot: HBV is not directly cytopathic. Many people carry high viral loads with little liver damage when the immune response is weak, as in neonatal infection.
Antibodies such as anti-HBs neutralize free virus, but antibody and complement are not the main cause of hepatocyte death.
HBsAg fills the endoplasmic reticulum in chronic carriers (ground-glass hepatocytes), but these cells are not killed by it.
Correct.

questions.stem: His partner completed the hepatitis B vaccine series 5 years ago. Her serology shows HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive, and total anti-HBc negative. Which of the following best explains the absence of anti-HBc?
options: Anti-HBc disappears within months after any exposure
The vaccine contains only recombinant HBsAg
Vaccine-induced anti-HBs neutralizes the core protein
The vaccine is a live virus that lacks the core gene
approach: Ask which viral proteins the vaccine contains.
The vaccine is recombinant HBsAg only, with no core protein.
So vaccination produces anti-HBs alone, while natural infection produces both anti-HBs and anti-HBc.
questions.why: The hepatitis B vaccine is a subunit vaccine of recombinant HBsAg produced in yeast. It teaches the immune system to make anti-HBs, which neutralizes the virus. Because no core antigen is given, vaccinated people never make anti-HBc. Anti-HBs alone therefore means vaccine immunity, while anti-HBs together with IgG anti-HBc means recovery from natural infection.
whyNot: IgG anti-HBc usually persists for life after natural infection. That is why it marks past infection.
Correct.
Anti-HBs binds the surface antigen. It does not neutralize or remove core protein, which is inside the virion.
The hepatitis B vaccine is not a live virus. It is a subunit vaccine of surface antigen made in yeast.

questions.stem: His serum bilirubin is raised in both the conjugated and unconjugated fractions. Which of the following best explains this pattern?
options: Accelerated heme breakdown from immune-mediated hemolysis
Inherited absence of hepatic UGT1A1 activity
Hepatocyte injury impairing conjugation and excretion
Extrahepatic obstruction of the common bile duct by a stone
approach: Indirect bilirubin is total minus direct: 6.2 minus 4.5 equals 1.7 mg/dL, so both fractions are high.
ALT above 1,000 U/L with only a small alkaline phosphatase rise is a hepatocellular pattern.
Injured hepatocytes take up and conjugate less bilirubin, and conjugated bilirubin leaks back into blood from damaged cells and canaliculi.
questions.why: In hepatitis, injured hepatocytes cannot take up, conjugate, and excrete bilirubin normally. Some unconjugated bilirubin is not processed, and conjugated bilirubin leaks back into the blood because excretion into bile is the slowest step. The result is a mixed hyperbilirubinemia with bilirubin in the urine. A very high ALT with a modest alkaline phosphatase distinguishes this from obstructive jaundice, where conjugated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase dominate.
whyNot: Hemolysis raises mainly unconjugated bilirubin, with no bilirubin in the urine. His dark urine and high direct fraction show conjugated bilirubin.
Absent UGT1A1 (Crigler-Najjar type I) causes severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia from birth with no conjugated rise.
Correct.
A common duct stone raises mainly conjugated bilirubin with a high alkaline phosphatase and pain. His transaminases are far higher than his alkaline phosphatase, which points to hepatocyte injury.

case: A 36-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of fever and right upper quadrant pain that radiates to the right shoulder. He returned 4 months ago from a year of agricultural work in rural southern Mexico, where he had bloody diarrhea for about a week. Temperature is 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg. Physical examination shows tender hepatomegaly and tenderness over the right lower intercostal spaces. Leukocyte count is 16,500/mm3 (normal 4,500 to 11,000) with no eosinophilia. Alkaline phosphatase is 210 U/L (normal 40 to 130). CT scan of the abdomen shows a single 7-cm abscess in the right lobe of the liver. Serum antibodies to Entamoeba histolytica are positive. Diagnosis: amebic liver abscess.

questions.stem: Aspiration of the abscess is performed. Which of the following findings in the aspirated fluid is most likely?
options: Foul-smelling pus containing gram-negative rods and anaerobes
Clear fluid containing daughter cysts and protoscolex hooklets
Reddish brown odorless fluid with no bacteria on Gram stain
Green bile-stained fluid with cholesterol crystals
approach: Travel to an endemic area, prior bloody diarrhea, a single right lobe abscess, and positive amebic serology point to amebic abscess.
Amebae dissolve liver tissue into a thick, odorless, reddish brown fluid often called anchovy paste.
The fluid is usually sterile on Gram stain and culture; trophozoites are found mainly in the abscess wall.
questions.why: Amebic liver abscess is a cavity of liquefied liver tissue made by Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites. The contents are reddish brown, odorless, and usually free of bacteria and neutrophils, because amebae lyse neutrophils. Pyogenic abscesses are often multiple, follow biliary infection or portal spread from bowel disease, and contain foul pus with enteric gram-negative rods or anaerobes. Travel history and serology help separate the two.
whyNot: Foul pus with mixed bacteria is the content of a pyogenic abscess, which usually comes from biliary disease or portal spread and grows E. coli, Klebsiella, or anaerobes.
Clear fluid with daughter cysts and hooklets is a hydatid cyst of Echinococcus granulosus, usually found in people exposed to dogs and sheep.
Correct.
Bile-stained fluid suggests a biloma from bile duct injury, not an abscess after amebic dysentery.

questions.stem: Which of the following would most likely have been found in an intestinal biopsy specimen during his diarrheal illness?
options: Flagellated trophozoites attached to villi without invasion
Flask-shaped ulcers with trophozoites containing red cells
Acid-fast oocysts on the brush border without ulceration
Rhabditiform larvae in crypts with eosinophilic infiltrates
approach: The liver abscess and earlier bloody diarrhea point to invasive Entamoeba histolytica.
Trophozoites invade the colonic mucosa and spread sideways in the submucosa, making flask-shaped ulcers.
The trophozoites often contain ingested red blood cells, which separates them from harmless amebae.
questions.why: Entamoeba histolytica is spread by cysts in fecally contaminated food and water. Trophozoites attack the colon, most often the cecum and ascending colon, and make narrow-necked, broad-based flask-shaped ulcers. They ingest red blood cells, and this is a key way to recognize them. From the ulcers, trophozoites can enter portal venous blood and reach the liver.
whyNot: Flagellated trophozoites stuck to villi without invasion describe Giardia, which causes fatty, nonbloody diarrhea from contaminated water.
Correct.
Acid-fast oocysts on the brush border are Cryptosporidium, which causes watery diarrhea, severe in people with advanced HIV infection.
Larvae in the crypts are Strongyloides, which penetrates skin and can cause hyperinfection with corticosteroid use.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most likely route by which trophozoites traveled from his colon to his liver?
options: Ileocolic lymphatics to the thoracic duct
Inferior vena cava to the hepatic veins
Common bile duct ascending from the duodenum
Superior mesenteric vein to portal vein
approach: Amebic ulcers are usually in the cecum and ascending colon, which drain to the superior mesenteric vein.
The superior mesenteric vein joins the splenic vein behind the pancreatic neck to form the portal vein.
Portal blood enters the liver first, so amebae lodge in the hepatic sinusoids.
questions.why: Venous blood from the cecum and ascending colon drains through the ileocolic and right colic veins to the superior mesenteric vein. It joins the splenic vein to form the portal vein, which delivers the blood to the liver sinusoids before it reaches the hepatic veins and inferior vena cava. Trophozoites in this blood are trapped in the liver. Flow from the superior mesenteric vein tends to stream into the right lobe, which helps explain why most amebic abscesses form there.
whyNot: Lymph from the colon drains to the thoracic duct and then the systemic veins, which would take organisms to the lungs first, not directly to the liver.
Blood in the inferior vena cava flows toward the heart. Hepatic veins drain the liver into the vena cava, not the other way.
Spread up the common bile duct is the route of ascending cholangitis and many pyogenic abscesses, not amebic abscess.
Correct.

topics: Portal venous drainage of the colon

questions.stem: During his diarrheal illness, stool studies would most likely have shown which of the following?
options: Bloody stool, low osmotic gap, persists with fasting
Watery stool, high osmotic gap, stops with fasting
Watery stool, low osmotic gap, persists with fasting
Greasy stool, high fecal fat, stops with fasting
approach: Invasive amebic colitis damages the mucosa and causes bloody stool: an inflammatory diarrhea.
Inflammatory diarrhea does not come from unabsorbed solutes, so the stool osmotic gap is low and fasting does not stop it.
Compare with osmotic diarrhea (high gap, stops with fasting) and secretory diarrhea (low gap, watery, persists).
questions.why: Diarrhea is grouped by mechanism. Osmotic diarrhea comes from unabsorbed solutes, so the stool osmotic gap is high (above about 100 to 125 mOsm/kg) and the diarrhea stops with fasting. Secretory diarrhea comes from active chloride secretion, as with cholera toxin, so the gap is low (below about 50 mOsm/kg) and it persists with fasting. Inflammatory diarrhea comes from mucosal damage, with blood in the stool, a low gap, and persistence with fasting. Amebic colitis is a classic inflammatory cause.
whyNot: Correct.
A high osmotic gap that stops with fasting is osmotic diarrhea, such as from lactose that is not absorbed.
Watery diarrhea with a low gap that continues during fasting is secretory diarrhea, as from cholera toxin raising cAMP and opening CFTR chloride channels. It is not bloody.
Greasy stool with high fecal fat is malabsorption, as in Giardia infection or pancreatic insufficiency, not invasive colitis.

dx: Lynch syndrome right-sided colon adenocarcinoma with liver metastasis
case: A 46-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of fatigue and shortness of breath on exertion. Her mother had endometrial cancer at the age of 49 years, and a maternal uncle had colon cancer at the age of 44 years. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows pallor. Hemoglobin is 8.6 g/dL (normal 12.0 to 16.0), mean corpuscular volume is 71 fL (normal 80 to 100), and serum ferritin is 6 ng/mL (normal 12 to 150). A test for fecal occult blood is positive. Colonoscopy shows an ulcerated mass in the ascending colon; biopsy shows poorly differentiated mucinous adenocarcinoma with many tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes. CT scan of the abdomen shows two solid masses in the liver. Diagnosis: Lynch syndrome with adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon.

questions.stem: Which of the following molecular findings is most likely in her tumor?
options: Biallelic APC loss with chromosomal instability
Microsatellite instability from mismatch repair loss
Germline STK11 mutation with hamartomatous polyps
Defective nucleotide excision repair of thymine dimers
approach: Early colon cancer and endometrial cancer in close relatives fit Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer).
Lynch syndrome is a germline defect in a DNA mismatch repair gene such as MLH1 or MSH2.
Without mismatch repair, replication errors build up in short repeated sequences, causing microsatellite instability.
questions.why: Lynch syndrome is autosomal dominant. Patients inherit one faulty mismatch repair gene (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2), and the second copy is lost in the tumor. Errors made when DNA polymerase slips on repetitive sequences are not fixed, so microsatellites change length, and mutations pile up in growth control genes. These cancers tend to be right-sided, mucinous, and full of lymphocytes. Sporadic cancers usually follow the APC, KRAS, TP53 adenoma to carcinoma sequence instead.
whyNot: APC loss followed by KRAS activation and TP53 loss is the chromosomal instability pathway of most sporadic cancers and of familial adenomatous polyposis, which presents with hundreds of polyps.
Correct.
STK11 mutations cause Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, with hamartomatous polyps and mucocutaneous pigmentation.
Nucleotide excision repair defects cause xeroderma pigmentosum, with skin cancers after sunlight exposure, not hereditary colon cancer.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why her tumor presented with iron deficiency anemia rather than bowel obstruction?
options: Annular napkin-ring growth typical of right colon tumors
Hemolysis induced by cytokines secreted by the tumor
Wide lumen and liquid stool in the right colon
Impaired duodenal iron absorption from liver metastases
approach: A microcytic anemia with low ferritin and occult blood points to slow bleeding from the colon.
The cecum and ascending colon have a wide lumen and liquid contents, so bulky tumors rarely block them.
These exophytic tumors ooze blood and present with iron deficiency anemia.
questions.why: Right-sided colon cancers tend to be bulky, polypoid masses in a wide segment filled with liquid stool. They bleed slowly and rarely obstruct, so iron deficiency anemia is a common first sign. Left-sided cancers often grow around the wall in a napkin-ring pattern in a narrow segment with formed stool, causing a change in bowel habit and obstruction. Iron deficiency anemia in an older man or a postmenopausal woman should prompt a search for colon cancer. CEA is used to watch for recurrence after treatment, not for screening.
whyNot: Annular napkin-ring growth is typical of left-sided cancers, which narrow the lumen and cause a change in bowel habit and obstruction.
Her anemia is microcytic with a very low ferritin, which shows iron loss from bleeding, not hemolysis.
Correct.
Iron is absorbed in the duodenum, and liver metastases do not block this. The low ferritin reflects chronic blood loss.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most likely nature of the liver masses?
options: Colorectal adenocarcinoma metastases
Primary hepatocellular carcinoma
Multiple cavernous hemangiomas
Hepatocellular adenomas from estrogen exposure
approach: Metastases are the most common malignant tumors of the liver, far outnumbering primary liver cancer.
Colon cancer drains through the portal vein, so the liver is the first capillary bed it reaches.
Multiple solid liver masses in a patient with colon cancer are metastases until proven otherwise.
questions.why: Metastatic tumors are much more common in the liver than primary cancers. Cancers of the colon, stomach, and pancreas reach the liver through portal venous blood, and breast and lung cancers reach it through the hepatic artery. Metastases are usually multiple. Among benign lesions, cavernous hemangioma is the most common, and hepatocellular adenoma is linked to estrogen or anabolic steroid exposure and carries a risk of rupture.
whyNot: Correct.
Hepatocellular carcinoma usually arises in a liver with cirrhosis or chronic HBV or HCV infection. Nothing in her history suggests either, and she has a known primary tumor.
Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor, but multiple solid masses in a patient with colon cancer are much more likely to be metastases.
Hepatocellular adenomas are linked to oral contraceptives and anabolic steroids and can rupture. With a known colon cancer, metastasis is far more likely.

questions.stem: During her evaluation she develops septic shock from a urinary tract infection, with a blood pressure near 72/40 mm Hg for several hours. Two days later she has left-sided abdominal pain and bloody stools, and colonoscopy shows ischemic mucosa limited to the splenic flexure. Which of the following best explains the vulnerability of this segment?
options: It is supplied by end arteries arising directly from the aorta
It receives its blood only from the superior rectal artery
It drains to the systemic rather than the portal venous system
It lies where superior and inferior mesenteric supply meet
approach: Ischemia after a period of hypotension affects watershed zones, where two arterial territories meet.
The superior mesenteric artery (middle colic) supplies the colon up to near the splenic flexure; the inferior mesenteric artery (left colic) supplies beyond it.
At the junction, the marginal artery is often thin, so this segment is the first to suffer when pressure falls.
questions.why: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut, from the duodenum to the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon. The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut beyond that. The marginal artery links the two along the colon, but at the splenic flexure the connection is often thin. When blood pressure falls, these border zones get the least flow. The splenic flexure and the rectosigmoid junction are the classic watershed sites for ischemic colitis.
whyNot: The splenic flexure is supplied by colic branches of the mesenteric arteries through the marginal artery, not by end arteries straight from the aorta.
The superior rectal artery, the end of the inferior mesenteric artery, supplies the upper rectum, not the splenic flexure.
The splenic flexure drains to the inferior mesenteric vein and the portal system. Venous drainage does not explain ischemia from low blood pressure.
Correct.
